passages.text: This guide describes the ORDIQ screens as they are in the current release. When an older document describes a screen differently, this guide is the current one.

The top bar shows the MSEUF logo, the term selector, the light/dark theme switch, the notifications bell, the Dean's name and the sign-out button. Every page shows data for the term chosen in the term selector.

The left sidebar has: Dashboard, Faculty, Courses & Sections, Rooms & Laboratories, Schedules, Rules & Preferences, Reports, AI Assistant and Settings. On phones the sidebar opens from the menu button at the top left.

The AI chat panel opens from the round ORDIQ button at the bottom right of the screen. On very wide screens it docks beside the page; on smaller screens it slides in as a drawer.

1. Open the sign-in page and enter the Dean username or email and the password.
2. If two-factor authentication is on, enter the 6-digit code from Google Authenticator (or another authenticator app). The first sign-in shows a QR code to scan and a set of single-use recovery codes to keep offline.
3. If two-factor authentication is turned off in Settings, the password alone signs in.

After too many wrong attempts the account locks for a while (by default 5 attempts and 15 minutes; both are set in Settings). Only one Dean account exists; there is no sign-up page.

To sign out, press the sign-out icon at the top right and confirm. ORDIQ also signs the Dean out automatically after a period of inactivity and after the maximum session length (see Settings).

Settings holds the system-wide switches. Every saved change is recorded in the audit log.

- Sign-in security: two-factor authentication (Google Authenticator) on or off; failed attempts before the account locks (3 to 10); lock duration (1 to 1,440 minutes). Turning two-factor off keeps the authenticator setup, so turning it back on needs no new QR scan.
- Session & automatic sign-out: sign out after inactivity (auto-expire) on or off; inactivity limit (5 to 480 minutes, default 30); maximum session length (1 to 72 hours, default 12).
- AI Assistant: turn the assistant on or off, and set the monthly token budget. When it is off, the chat button, the AI Assistant page and the AI menu item are hidden and nothing is sent to the AI provider.
- Server configuration: read-only status of the web app, the scheduling engine and the AI provider.

Changes appear in a save bar at the bottom of the page. Sign-in and session changes need the current password before they can be saved; the password box turns red if Save is pressed without it. "Discard" undoes unsaved edits and "Restore recommended values" resets the switches to the defaults.

The Dashboard shows four figures for the selected term: Classes Scheduled (out of the total meetings), Conflicts Detected, Faculty Load Balance (out of 100) and Room Utilization (percent). Hovering a figure shows how it is calculated. Below them are tabs for the schedule, faculty data, courses and sections, and rooms and labs.

The Faculty page lists the engineering faculty with their employment type (Full-Time Permanent, Full-Time Contract, Part-Time or Visiting) and load limits. Opening a faculty member shows three areas:

- Availability: days and time windows when the faculty member is available or unavailable, with a reason.
- Qualifications: the subjects the faculty member can teach and whether they have taught them before.
- Preferences: preferred days, times or rooms, with a weight and a source (faculty survey, set by the Dean, or learned from history).

This page has three tabs: Subjects Catalog (subject codes, units, lecture and laboratory hours), Student Sections (section codes and their student counts only; ORDIQ keeps no individual student records) and Course Offerings (which subject is offered to which section this term). Programs and terms are managed here too.
This page lists lecture rooms and laboratories with their type, capacity and availability, including maintenance periods when a room cannot be used.

Master data can be typed in on each page or imported from the official Excel workbook. An import is checked first (a dry run) and every row or column problem is reported in plain words before anything is saved.

The Schedules page is the schedule workspace.

- Generate (CP-SAT): creates three candidate schedules for the term: Candidate A (Balanced), Candidate B (Faculty First) and Candidate C (Student First). Every candidate is checked again by the independent validator against hard rules HC-01 to HC-15.
- Views: an hourly schedule grid and day column cards, filterable by section, faculty, room and weekday.
- Editing: a meeting can be moved to another day, time, room or faculty member. Each edit is validated right away and conflicts are shown with the rule explained in plain words. "Undo Edit" reverses the last change.
- Check Schedule: runs the validator again on the open schedule.
- Compare: shows the candidates side by side (quality score, conflicts, unscheduled meetings).
- Waived exceptions: a waivable rule (HC-04 to HC-15) can be overridden with a written reason. Double booking of a faculty member, room or section (HC-01, HC-02, HC-03) can never be waived.
- Accept Candidate: makes a candidate the official schedule. ORDIQ only accepts a candidate with zero unwaived hard conflicts and zero unscheduled meetings. Accepting archives the previously accepted schedule for the term.
- Start Schedule Revision: creates a new draft from the accepted schedule so it can be edited without touching the accepted version.
- Import / Export: bring in an existing schedule or export the open one.

This page has five tabs:

- Hard Constraints: the fixed rules HC-01 to HC-15 that every schedule must meet. The rules themselves cannot be edited; the "Adjust In" column links to the page where each rule's inputs are changed (for example room capacity on Rooms & Laboratories, or faculty availability on Faculty).
- Objective Weights: how much each soft preference (SC-01 to SC-16) counts when the solver builds candidates.
- Dean Directives: extra rules for the next generation run, such as keeping a faculty member off a day, a time window for a section, avoiding or requiring a room, pinning a meeting, assigning a faculty member, or changing a weight. Each directive is hard or soft.
- Locked Fixed Blocks: time blocks that are already taken, such as classes run by other departments (General Education, PATHFIT, NSTP) or college events.
- Readiness Gate: the data readiness check (ISO/IEC 25012: completeness, accuracy, consistency, currentness). Critical gaps block schedule generation until they are fixed.

At the top of the Reports page, Schedule used in the reports picks which schedule the reports are built from. It starts on the accepted schedule; a draft candidate can be chosen instead, and its reports then carry a "not official" notice. Reports are grouped as follows. Class timetables: Schedule per Section, per Faculty and per Room, each grouped by section, faculty member or room in day and time order, with a filter to print just one section, faculty member or room. Load and utilization: Faculty Load and Room Utilization. Summary and compliance: College Schedule Summary, Conflicts and Exceptions (problems to fix, approved exceptions with their reasons, classes not scheduled), Data Quality and Preferences, and Candidate Comparison (the accepted schedule and all draft candidates side by side). Working files, Excel only: Portal Encoding Export and Revision History. View PDF opens a printable PDF in a new tab; Download Excel saves an .xlsx file. The Portal Encoding Export is laid out for the scheduling officer to encode manually; ORDIQ never connects to the university portal itself.

The AI Assistant page has four tabs:

- Briefing: the term's figures (Scheduled, Conflicts, Unscheduled, Pending proposals), an optional AI summary, and a "Needs attention" list with links to where each issue is fixed.
- Proposals: changes the assistant proposed. Each shows the meeting now and the proposed slot, the quality change and whether it creates a conflict. Only the Dean can Apply or Reject a proposal.
- History: past conversations for the term, with search; a conversation can be continued in the chat panel or deleted.
- Usage: the AI provider and model in use, the tokens used against the monthly budget, the estimated cost, and the faculty matching model with its accuracy and a Retrain button.

The chat panel answers questions about the selected term in English, Filipino or Taglish, using the live schedule data. The menu (three dots) starts a new conversation or opens a recent one. The assistant can check conflicts, summarize loads and room use, explain unscheduled classes, find alternative slots, recommend faculty, add directives, generate new candidates and propose a change. It cannot apply a proposal, accept a schedule, delete records, edit master data or create accounts; those stay with the Dean in the workspace. Faculty names are replaced with codes before anything is sent to the AI provider and restored in the reply.

The bell at the top shows how many urgent or warning items need attention for the selected term: data problems that block generation, no schedule yet, conflicts, unscheduled classes, faculty overloads and proposals waiting for review. Opening the bell lists each item with a link to fix it. "Mark all as read" clears the count; an item comes back as unread if it changes, and disappears once the problem is resolved. Read status is kept per browser.
Short answers to the questions the Dean asks most. Each entry lists other ways the question is asked, in English, Filipino and Taglish.

passages.section: How do I sign in to ORDIQ?
passages.text:
Also asked: paano mag-login, how to log in, sign in steps.

Enter the Dean username or email and the password on the sign-in page. If two-factor authentication is on, enter the 6-digit code from the authenticator app next. Only the Dean has an account; there is no sign-up page.

passages.section: What if I lose my phone with Google Authenticator?
passages.text:
Also asked: nawala ang phone, lost authenticator, cannot get the 6-digit code, recovery code.

On the code step of sign-in, choose "Use a recovery code" and enter one of the single-use recovery codes shown when two-factor was first set up. Each recovery code works once. If no recovery codes are left, the system administrator can reset the Dean account with the seed script described in the Operations manual.

passages.section: How do I turn two-factor authentication on or off?
passages.text:
Also asked: paano i-off ang 2FA, i-on ang Google Authenticator, disable TOTP, enable authenticator.

Open Settings, go to Sign-in security, and switch "Two-factor authentication (Google Authenticator)". Saving needs the current password. Turning it off keeps the authenticator setup, so turning it back on later needs no new QR scan. With it off, anyone who learns the password can sign in.

Also asked: na-lock ang account, locked out, too many attempts, maling password.

After a number of wrong sign-in attempts in a row the account locks for a set time. The defaults are 5 attempts and 15 minutes. Wait for the lock to end and try again. Both numbers are set in Settings › Sign-in security (3 to 10 attempts, 1 to 1,440 minutes).

passages.section: Why was I signed out automatically?
passages.text:
Also asked: bakit na-logout, auto logout, session expired, auto-expire, kusang nag-sign out.

ORDIQ signs the Dean out after a period of inactivity (default 30 minutes) and after the maximum session length (default 12 hours). Both are set in Settings › Session & automatic sign-out, where the inactivity sign-out can also be turned off.

passages.section: Why does saving settings ask for my password?
passages.text:
Also asked: bakit hinihingi ang password sa settings, current password required.

Changes to sign-in security and automatic sign-out protect the account, so ORDIQ asks for the current password before saving them. AI Assistant settings save without it. Every saved change is recorded in the audit log.

passages.section: How do I turn off the AI Assistant?
passages.text:
Also asked: i-disable ang AI, patayin ang chatbot, turn off chat.

Open Settings › AI Assistant and switch it off, then save. The chat button, the AI Assistant page and its sidebar item disappear and nothing is sent to the AI provider. The rest of ORDIQ keeps working.

passages.section: What is the monthly token budget?
passages.text:
Also asked: token limit, AI budget, gaano karami ang tokens.

It caps how much the AI Assistant can use each month. When it is used up, the assistant falls back to ORDIQ's built-in answers until the next month. The budget is set in Settings › AI Assistant and usage is shown on AI Assistant › Usage.

passages.section: How do I create a schedule for the term?
passages.text:
Also asked: paano gumawa ng schedule, generate schedule steps, saan magsisimula, where do I start for a new term, first steps.

1. Make sure the term's data is complete: faculty, subjects, sections, offerings and rooms. The Readiness Gate on Rules & Preferences shows what is missing.
2. Open Schedules and press Generate (CP-SAT). ORDIQ creates three candidates: Balanced, Faculty First and Student First.
3. Review and compare them, fix any conflicts or unscheduled meetings, then accept one.

passages.section: What is the difference between Balanced, Faculty First and Student First?
passages.text:
Also asked: candidate A B C, ano ang pinagkaiba ng candidates, weight profiles.

They are three candidate schedules built from the same data with different weights on the soft preferences. Candidate A (Balanced) keeps the weights moderate across faculty and student preferences. Candidate B (Faculty First) weighs faculty preferred days and times (SC-01), load balance (SC-02), preferred rooms (SC-04) and faculty fit (SC-07) more heavily. Candidate C (Student First) weighs fewer gaps (SC-03), an even spread across the week (SC-05), no evening classes for lower years (SC-09), lower-year priority (SC-10), no late laboratories (SC-11) and spreading major subjects (SC-12) more heavily. All three must meet the same hard rules.

Also asked: bakit may unscheduled, hindi nailagay na klase, unplaced meetings.

When a meeting cannot be placed without breaking a hard rule, ORDIQ leaves it unscheduled and states the reason instead of failing the whole schedule. Common reasons are no qualified faculty available, no free room of the right type or size, or the section's time already taken. The Schedules page and the assistant list each unscheduled meeting with its reason.

passages.section: How do I fix a conflict?
passages.text:
Also asked: paano ayusin ang conflict, resolve violation, may banggaan sa schedule.

Open the schedule on the Schedules page and move the meeting to another day, time, room or faculty member; each edit is checked right away. The assistant can also find conflict-free alternative slots or propose a change for the Dean to apply. If the rule is waivable (HC-04 to HC-15) and the situation is intended, record a waived exception with a written reason.

passages.section: How do I accept a schedule?
passages.text:
Also asked: paano i-accept ang schedule, approve the candidate, gawing official.

On the Schedules page, open the candidate and press Accept Candidate, then confirm. ORDIQ accepts it only when it has zero unwaived hard conflicts and zero unscheduled meetings. Accepting archives any previously accepted schedule for the term. "Accepted" means approved for portal encoding; university approval happens outside ORDIQ.

passages.section: Why can't I accept the schedule?
passages.text:
Also asked: ayaw ma-accept, hindi ma-accept ang candidate, accept failed.

ORDIQ blocks acceptance while the candidate still has unwaived hard conflicts or unscheduled meetings. Fix or waive the conflicts (only HC-04 to HC-15 can be waived) and place the remaining meetings, then accept again.

passages.section: Can the AI Assistant accept a schedule or apply a change?
passages.text:
Also asked: kaya ba ng chatbot mag-accept, can the AI apply proposals.

No. The assistant can check, explain, generate candidates, add directives and propose a change, but it has no way to apply a proposal, accept a schedule, delete records or edit master data. The Dean does those in the workspace, and proposals are applied or rejected on AI Assistant › Proposals.

passages.section: How do I change an accepted schedule?
passages.text:
Also asked: paano mag-revise, edit accepted schedule, may babaguhin sa accepted.

Open the accepted schedule and press Start Schedule Revision. ORDIQ creates a new draft version from it, so edits never change the accepted version. Accept the revision when it is ready.

passages.section: How do I undo an edit?
passages.text:
Also asked: i-undo, balik sa dati, revert change.

On the Schedules page, press Undo Edit to reverse the last change to the open schedule.

Also asked: waive, documented exception, override a rule.

A waived exception lets a waivable hard rule (HC-04 to HC-15) be broken on purpose, with a written reason that is kept in the record and shown in the Conflicts and Exceptions report. Double booking of a faculty member, room or section (HC-01, HC-02, HC-03) can never be waived.

Also asked: ano ang directive, add a rule for the next run.

A directive is an extra rule the Dean adds for the next generation run. The types are: keep a faculty member off a day, a time window for a faculty member or a section, avoid a room, require a room, pin a meeting, assign a faculty member, and change a preference weight. Each is hard (must hold) or soft (preferred). Directives are on Rules & Preferences › Dean Directives, and the assistant can add one from a chat request. They do not change existing schedules until candidates are generated again.

Also asked: fixed blocks, GenEd, PATHFIT, NSTP, klase ng ibang department.

Fixed blocks are time slots a section already uses for classes the college does not schedule, such as General Education, PATHFIT, NSTP or classes in other buildings. ORDIQ keeps those sections free at those times (HC-15). They are managed on Rules & Preferences › Locked Fixed Blocks.

passages.section: What does the Readiness Gate check?
passages.text:
Also asked: data readiness, kulang na data, ready na ba mag-generate, ISO 25012.

It checks the term's data for completeness, accuracy, consistency and currentness (ISO/IEC 25012) before generation. Critical gaps block generation until they are fixed, for example a term with no offerings, a subject with no qualified faculty, a section larger than every suitable room, or more required hours than the faculty or rooms can cover. Warnings, such as missing faculty availability or an outdated curriculum record, do not block.

passages.section: How do I import data from Excel?
passages.text:
Also asked: paano mag-import, upload workbook, Excel template.

Use the Import button on the data page and choose the completed ORDIQ data-gathering workbook (.xlsx). ORDIQ checks the file first and lists every problem by row and column in plain words; nothing is saved until the check passes.

passages.section: Where do I set when a faculty member is available?
passages.text:
Also asked: availability ng faculty, hindi pwede ang guro sa araw na ito.

Open Faculty, select the faculty member and use Availability to add available or unavailable days and time windows with a reason. HC-06 keeps classes inside them.

passages.section: Where do I set what subjects a faculty member can teach?
passages.text:
Also asked: qualifications, specialization, anong subject ang kaya ng guro.

Open Faculty, select the faculty member and use Qualifications to add subjects. HC-09 only assigns faculty to subjects they are qualified for. The faculty matching model also uses this to recommend faculty.

passages.section: Where do I change room capacity or type?
passages.text:
Also asked: kapasidad ng kwarto, room size, lecture or laboratory.

Open Rooms & Laboratories and edit the room. Capacity is checked by HC-04 and the room type (lecture or laboratory) by HC-05.

Also asked: may student data ba, individual students, student ID.

No. ORDIQ stores only the number of students per section (decision D-21). There are no individual student names, IDs, grades or schedules anywhere in the system.

passages.section: Are faculty names sent to the AI provider?
passages.text:
Also asked: privacy ng faculty, pinapadala ba ang pangalan sa AI.

No. Before anything leaves ORDIQ, faculty names are replaced with codes such as ALIAS-001, and the real names are put back only in the reply shown to the Dean. Contact details, notes and raw imports are never sent.

passages.section: How do I export the schedule for the university portal?
passages.text:
Also asked: paano i-export, portal encoding, Excel para sa portal.

Open Reports and download the Portal Encoding Export (Excel). It is laid out for the scheduling officer to encode manually. ORDIQ never connects to the university portal directly.

Also asked: anong reports, download PDF, print schedule, print one faculty schedule, print a section's schedule.

Class timetables (Schedule per Section, per Faculty and per Room), Faculty Load, Room Utilization, College Schedule Summary, Conflicts and Exceptions, Data Quality and Preferences, Candidate Comparison, and two Excel-only working files: the Portal Encoding Export and Revision History. On the Reports page, choose the schedule at the top (the accepted one by default), then use View PDF or Download Excel on a report. To print one section, faculty member or room, pick it in the filter on that timetable card first.

passages.section: How is Faculty Load Balance calculated?
passages.text:
Also asked: load balance score, paano kinukuha ang faculty load balance.

It is 100 minus the spread (standard deviation) of faculty load utilization, where each faculty member's utilization is assigned units divided by their regular maximum units. 100 means every faculty member carries the same share of their limit; lower means loads are uneven. It appears on the Dashboard; hovering the figure shows the formula.

Also asked: best schedule ba ito, optimal, pinakamaganda ba.

The solver minimizes a weighted sum of soft-preference penalties, with a large penalty for every unscheduled meeting. "Proven optimal" means no better schedule exists for those weights; "best found" means the time limit ended the search. It does not mean a global best for every possible priority.

passages.section: How does the faculty recommendation work?
passages.text:
Also asked: ML, machine learning, faculty matching model, recommended faculty.

A logistic regression model scores how well each qualified faculty member fits a subject, using past assignments, qualifications and preferences. With little history it falls back to text similarity between subject and expertise. It only recommends; it never overrides a hard rule. The model can be retrained on AI Assistant › Usage.

Also asked: bell, notification count, needs attention.

The bell counts urgent and warning items for the selected term: data problems that block generation, no schedule yet, conflicts, unscheduled classes, faculty overloads and proposals awaiting review. Each item links to where it is fixed. "Mark all as read" clears the count until an item changes.

Also asked: sino ang pwedeng gumamit, coordinator account, multiple users.

Only the Dean signs in. Program coordinators and the scheduling officer work from the exported PDF and Excel reports. There is no sign-up page; the account is created by the administrator.

Also asked: ano ang ORDIQ, what does the system do, purpose.

ORDIQ ("Order Meets Intelligence") is the class scheduling and resource allocation system of the MSEUF College of Engineering. It builds candidate schedules with a constraint solver, checks every schedule with an independent validator, recommends faculty with machine learning, and offers a chat assistant in English, Filipino and Taglish. The Dean makes every final decision.

Also asked: list the hard rules, mandatory rules, HC list, ano ang mga hard constraints.

Every schedule must meet fifteen hard rules. HC-01 a faculty member teaches one class at a time. HC-02 a room hosts one class at a time. HC-03 a section attends one class at a time. HC-04 room capacity fits the section. HC-05 room type matches (lecture or laboratory). HC-06 faculty only when available. HC-07 faculty within maximum load. HC-08 all required meetings and hours scheduled. HC-09 faculty qualified for the subject. HC-10 rooms only when available. HC-11 inside allowed hours and outside official breaks. HC-12 required Dean directives respected. HC-13 required duration and meeting pattern. HC-14 calendar and maintenance restrictions. HC-15 sections clear of their fixed blocks. HC-01 to HC-03 can never be waived; the rest can be waived with a written reason. They are listed on Rules & Preferences › Hard Constraints.

passages.section: What languages does the assistant understand?
passages.text:
Also asked: Tagalog, Filipino, Taglish, English, pwede bang mag-Tagalog.

The AI Assistant understands and replies in English, Filipino and Taglish, and answers in the language of the question.

passages.section: HC-01: A faculty member teaches one class at a time
passages.text:
Also asked: faculty double booking, sabay na klase ng guro.

A faculty member cannot have two classes at the same time. Never waivable. Fix it on the Schedules page by moving one meeting or assigning another faculty member.

passages.section: HC-02: A room hosts one class at a time
passages.text:
Also asked: room double booking, dalawang klase sa isang kwarto.

A room cannot hold two classes at the same time. Never waivable. Fix it on the Schedules page by moving one meeting to another time or room.

passages.section: HC-03: A section attends one class at a time
passages.text:
Also asked: section double booking, sabay na klase ng section.

A section cannot have two classes at the same time. Never waivable. Fix it on the Schedules page.

passages.section: HC-04: Room capacity fits the section
passages.text:
Also asked: masyadong maliit ang kwarto, capacity.

The room must seat the section's student count. Waivable with a reason. Adjust room capacity on Rooms & Laboratories or section counts on Courses & Sections.

passages.section: HC-05: Room type matches the requirement
passages.text:
Also asked: laboratory sa lecture room, room type.

Laboratory meetings need a laboratory and lecture meetings a lecture room. Waivable with a reason. Room types are set on Rooms & Laboratories.

passages.section: HC-06: Faculty are scheduled only when available
passages.text:
Also asked: faculty availability conflict.

Classes must fall inside the faculty member's available time. Waivable with a reason. Availability is set on the Faculty page.

passages.section: HC-07: Faculty stay within maximum teaching load
passages.text:
Also asked: overload, sobra ang units.

A faculty member's units may not exceed the maximum for their employment type. Waivable with a reason. Load limits are on the Faculty page.

passages.section: HC-08: All required meetings and contact hours are scheduled
passages.text:
Also asked: kulang ang oras, missing meetings.

Every offering gets all its required meetings and contact hours. Waivable with a reason. Offerings are on Courses & Sections.

passages.section: HC-09: Faculty specialization matches the subject
passages.text:
Also asked: hindi qualified ang guro.

Faculty teach only subjects they are qualified for. Waivable with a reason. Qualifications are on the Faculty page.

passages.section: HC-10: Rooms are used only when available
passages.text:
Also asked: room not available.

Classes may use a room only during its available times. Waivable with a reason. Room availability is on Rooms & Laboratories.

passages.section: HC-11: Classes stay inside allowed periods and avoid official breaks
passages.text:
Also asked: lunch break, sobrang aga o gabi.

Classes must fall within the term's allowed hours and avoid official breaks. Waivable with a reason. Term hours are on Courses & Sections.

passages.section: HC-12: Required Dean directives are respected
passages.text:
Also asked: hard directive.

Directives marked hard must hold in every candidate. Waivable with a reason. Directives are on Rules & Preferences › Dean Directives.

passages.section: HC-13: Each class follows its required duration and meeting pattern
passages.text:
Also asked: meeting pattern, duration.

Each meeting keeps its required length and day pattern. Waivable with a reason. Patterns come from the offering on Courses & Sections.

passages.section: HC-14: Calendar and maintenance restrictions are respected
passages.text:
Also asked: maintenance, holiday.

Rooms under maintenance and restricted calendar periods are not used. Waivable with a reason. Maintenance periods are on Rooms & Laboratories.

passages.section: HC-15: Sections stay clear of their fixed blocks
passages.text:
Also asked: GenEd conflict, PATHFIT conflict.

A section's locked fixed blocks (classes run by other departments) stay free. Waivable with a reason. Fixed blocks are on Rules & Preferences › Locked Fixed Blocks.

Also asked: soft constraints, preferences, objective weights.

SC-01 honor faculty preferred days and times. SC-02 balance teaching loads. SC-03 minimize vacant gaps for faculty and sections. SC-04 use preferred rooms. SC-05 distribute classes evenly across the week. SC-06 minimize changes from the existing schedule when regenerating. SC-07 prefer faculty with a high ML fit score. SC-08 use rooms efficiently, such as not putting 15 students in a 40-seat room. Their weights are set on Rules & Preferences › Objective Weights; a preference counts only once it is approved.

Also asked: student preferences, survey preferences.

From the manuscript and student survey: SC-09 avoid evening classes for lower-year sections. SC-10 give lower-year sections priority. SC-11 keep laboratories away from late hours. SC-12 spread major and mathematics subjects across days. SC-13 keep a break between long back-to-back classes. SC-14 avoid a late class followed by an early class the next day. SC-15 place PATHFIT late in the day or before a vacant period. SC-16 limit very early starts. Each needs approval before it counts, and some pull against each other.

System: ORDIQ ("Order Meets Intelligence")  
Target Users: Dean of the College of Engineering (System Operator) & Scheduling Officer (Portal Encoder)

1. Navigate to `/login`.
2. Enter your Dean email (`[email removed]`), password, and the 6-digit TOTP Authenticator code from your mobile authenticator app.
3. Keep your single-use recovery codes in a secure offline location.

passages.section: 2. Step-by-Step Scheduling Workflow › Step 1: Import or Update Term Master Data
passages.text:
1. Open Faculty, Courses & Sections, Rooms & Laboratories, or Rules & Preferences from the left sidebar.
2. Download the official template (`templates/ordiq-data-gathering-workbook.xlsx`) or upload your completed `.xlsx` workbook.
3. ORDIQ runs a dry-run validation first, reporting any row/column errors in plain language before committing atomically.
4. Review the ISO/IEC 25012 Data Readiness Card (Completeness, Accuracy, Consistency, Currentness). Critical gaps block schedule generation until resolved.

passages.section: 2. Step-by-Step Scheduling Workflow › Step 2: Check Existing Schedule or Generate Candidates
passages.text:
1. Open Schedules (`/schedules`).
2. Click Generate 3 Candidates (CP-SAT) to produce three optimized candidate schedules:
   - Candidate A — Balanced (`BALANCED`)
   - Candidate B — Faculty First (`FACULTY_FIRST`)
   - Candidate C — Student First (`STUDENT_FIRST`)
3. Every candidate is independently re-validated by the Python validator against `HC-01` through `HC-15`.

passages.section: 2. Step-by-Step Scheduling Workflow › Step 3: Review, Edit, Waive, or Compare
passages.text:
1. Switch between the Spreadsheet Grid, Weekly Timetable Calendar (filtered by Section, Faculty, or Room), and Side-by-Side Candidate Comparison.
2. Click Pin/Unpin on any entry you want to lock in place before regenerating.
3. If a waivable rule (`HC-04` to `HC-15`) requires an administrative override, record a Documented Exception (`D-18`) with a written justification. Core double-booking rules (`HC-01` Faculty, `HC-02` Room, `HC-03` Section) can never be waived.
4. Click Accept Candidate for Portal Encoding once `0` unwaived hard conflicts and `0` unscheduled meetings remain.

passages.section: 3. Using the Conversational AI Assistant (English, Filipino & Taglish)
passages.text:
Open the persistent right panel or `/assistant` to give instructions in English, Filipino, or Taglish:
- *"Check schedule conflicts for Engr. Maria Clara Santos"*
- *"Kumusta ang room utilization at lab usage natin?"*
- *"Sino ang bagay magturo ng CPE-101 ayon sa specialization?"*

passages.section: 4. Known Limitations & Future Enhancements (For Thesis Manuscript)
passages.text:
1. Section-Level Representation (`D-21`): ORDIQ models student cohorts at the block/section level (`Section.studentCount`). Individual irregular students taking cross-year subjects are outside scope and are recommended under *Future Enhancements*.
2. Single-Semester Historical Baseline: With one semester of historical data (`1st Sem A.Y. 2026–2027`), the ML module uses cold-start local text similarity combined with regularized logistic regression and improves incrementally as future semesters are accepted.
3. Standalone Decision-Support Boundary: ORDIQ produces non-official candidate schedules and portal-ready Excel exports; official registration and student release remain in the MSEUF portal after Registrar, Audit, and OVPAR approval.

System: ORDIQ ("Order Meets Intelligence")  
Quotation Reference: `Q-2026-002`  
Compliance Alignment: Philippine Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA 10173), ISO/IEC 25010, ISO/IEC 25012

1. Zero Individual Student Records: ORDIQ operates strictly at the section level (`Section.studentCount`, e.g., `CE-1A: 38 students`). No database table, API endpoint, or Excel import sheet accepts or stores student names, student ID numbers, or individual student schedules.
2. Faculty Pseudonymization (`Faculty.alias`): Every faculty member is assigned a sequential pseudonym (`ALIAS-001`, `ALIAS-002`, etc.) stored in the database.

All Generative AI interactions pass through a single module (`apps/web/src/server/modules/ai/privacy-gateway.ts`), enforced by ESLint import boundaries:

1. Outgoing Scrubbing: Full names, surnames, given names, honorific combinations (`Engr.`, `Dr.`, `Prof.`, `Sir`, `Ma'am`), diacritic/accent variations (`Ñ` -> `N`, `á` -> `a`), and fuzzy misspellings next to honorifics (`Prof. Sntos` -> `ALIAS-001`) are replaced with `Faculty.alias` before any request leaves the application.
2. Allowlist Tool Serialization: Tool results are filtered through an explicit key allowlist (`serializeToolResultForLlm`). Free-text notes, email addresses, and contact numbers are never sent to the LLM.
3. Streaming De-Pseudonymization: `DePseudonymizerStream` buffers trailing partial tokens across chunk boundaries and restores real faculty names only inside the Dean's authenticated browser response.
4. Token-Only Usage Logging: `LlmUsageRecord` logs only `provider`, `model`, `tokensIn`, `tokensOut`, and `estimatedCostPhp`—never prompt or reply content.
5. Automated Egress Verification: Verified by the 32-prompt golden evaluation suite (`phase4-and-phase5-exit-criteria.test.ts`), asserting 0 faculty names in any captured LLM request payload.

- Dean-Only Access (`D-20`): Public signup is disabled. Every `/api/v1/*` data, generation, schedule, AI, ML, analytics, report, and evaluation endpoint requires an authenticated Dean session verified with Argon2id + TOTP 2FA.
- Append-Only Audit Log: Every state-changing action (`TERM_UPDATED`, `IMPORT_COMMITTED`, `GENERATION_RUN_COMPLETED`, `SCHEDULE_ENTRY_EDITED`, `SCHEDULE_EXCEPTION_ADDED`, `SCHEDULE_ACCEPTED`, `AI_PROPOSAL_APPLIED`, `ML_MODEL_TRAIN`, `REPORT_EXPORTED`) is recorded in the append-only `AuditLog`.

In accordance with Quotation `Q-2026-002`:
- Development and automated testing were conducted using synthetic fixtures (`generateSmallFixture` and `generateMediumCollegeFixture` modeling 7 programs, 44 faculty, and 903 students across 24 sections).
- Upon final turnover and acceptance, all copies of MSEUF College of Engineering schedules or faculty data on developer machines are permanently deleted and confirmed in writing.

System: ORDIQ ("Order Meets Intelligence") — AI-Based Class Scheduling Decision-Support System  
Client: College of Engineering, Manuel S. Enverga University Foundation (MSEUF), Lucena City  
Quotation Reference: `Q-2026-002`

passages.section: 1. Starting and Stopping the System › Network Isolation
passages.text:
- Only `apps/web` (port `3000` behind TLS reverse proxy) is exposed to the network.
- `services/engine` (port `8000`) and `postgres` (port `5432`) run on an internal Docker bridge network with no public internet exposure, and every Web → Engine call requires the shared `X-Engine-Token` header.

passages.section: 2. Seeding or Resetting the Dean Account
passages.text:
Public account registration is permanently disabled (`D-20`). The Dean's account is managed exclusively via the CLI seed script:

- Passwords are hashed using Argon2id.
- First login requires TOTP 2FA enrollment (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, or Authy) and generates single-use recovery codes.
- TOTP secrets are encrypted at rest using AES-256-GCM with `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.

ORDIQ supports switching LLM providers via `.env` without any code changes (`D-09`):

- Cloud (Standard Package): Set `LLM_PROVIDER=openai` (with `OPENAI_API_KEY`) or `LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic` (with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`).
- On-Premise Local (Premium / Offline Mode): Set `LLM_PROVIDER=ollama` and `OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://ollama:11434`.
- Regardless of provider, all traffic passes through the Privacy Gateway (`src/server/modules/ai/privacy-gateway.ts`), which replaces all faculty names with `Faculty.alias` (`ALIAS-001`, etc.) before egress.

passages.section: 5. Secret Rotation Checklist for Production Turnover
passages.text:
Before live use with MSEUF College of Engineering data:
1. Generate a fresh 64-hex-character `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (`openssl rand -hex 32`).
2. Generate a fresh `ENGINE_TOKEN` (`openssl rand -hex 32`) and update both `apps/web` and `services/engine`.
3. Generate a fresh `SESSION_SECRET` (`openssl rand -hex 32`).
4. Set `DEAN_INITIAL_PASSWORD` and run `pnpm --filter @ordiq/web db:seed-dean` so the Dean enrolls their own TOTP device.

The Dean tells a GPT-style assistant what is needed, and ORDIQ validates the data, generates conflict-free candidate schedules, and helps compare them before anything is encoded in the university portal. People no longer build the timetable by hand and hunt for conflicts afterward.

The manuscript's root-cause finding is "insufficiently systematic early validation, compounded by changing data and manual handoffs." So validation and rechecking after changes matter as much as generation.

| Item | Fact from the manuscript |
|---|---|
| Scope | Seven programs (Civil, Computer, Electrical, Electronics, Geodetic, Industrial, Mechanical) in the current College of Engineering building |
| Faculty | 44: 12 full-time permanent, 18 full-time non-permanent, 13 part-time, 1 visiting |
| Students | 903 first- and second-year students. ORDIQ uses section-level counts only, with no individual student records |
| Stakeholders | Dean, 7 program coordinators, scheduling officer |
| Manual baseline | 47 days: 15 for plotting, 22 for rework and portal encoding (not separable), 10 for university review |
| Rooms | Lecture rooms hold at least 40 students, laboratories at least 30 |
| Interview ranking of challenges | 1. Faculty specialization, 2. Time gaps between subjects, 3. Room and laboratory use by capacity |
| Most reported problem | Classroom conflicts (19 selections from 23 faculty) |
| Time signals, unverified | Survey comments mention 7:30 AM starts, classes ending 8:30 PM, a 12:00 to 1:30 break, and six-day weeks |
| Outside the system | Portal encoding, approval by the Registrar, Audit and OVPAR, student change requests, release to students |

| # | Criterion | Measured by |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A generated candidate has zero hard constraint violations | Independent validator on every saved schedule |
| 2 | Candidates are compared fairly with the first-semester A.Y. 2026-2027 schedule | Side-by-side report: conflicts, gaps, load balance, utilization, preferences met |
| 3 | The Dean can generate and adjust a schedule in plain language, including Taglish | Scripted acceptance scenarios |
| 4 | Machine learning visibly improves results over time | Recommendation metrics per model version, plus a demonstrable change after Dean edits |
| 5 | Only the Dean can access the system, and no faculty names reach the AI provider | Access tests and the privacy egress test |
| 6 | Dashboards and PDF/Excel reports use the same numbers | One analytics service feeds all of them |
| 7 | The system produces the evidence for the paper's three evaluation stages | Evaluation records and export (Phase 7) |

No performance improvement is claimed until it is tested. This is the manuscript's own rule, so the UI, docs and demos follow it too.

`FACULTY_NOT_ON_DAY`, `FACULTY_TIME_WINDOW`, `SECTION_TIME_WINDOW`, `AVOID_ROOM`, `REQUIRE_ROOM`, `PIN_MEETING`, `ASSIGN_FACULTY`, `SET_WEIGHT`.

If a request does not fit one of these, the assistant says so and does not improvise.

The manuscript defines optimization as improving schedule quality and resource use against the documented baseline. It "does not imply a mathematically global optimum," and feasibility alone doesn't prove quality.

The objective is the weighted sum of soft penalties, plus a very large penalty per unscheduled meeting. The manuscript leaves open whether priorities are weights or a strict order, so this needs a decision (Q-12).

- Proven optimal: the solver finished and proved no better schedule exists for these weights.
- Best found: the time limit ended the search, and the solver reports the remaining gap.

The UI shows which one applies, plus which preferences went unmet. Don't describe every result as "the best possible."

Objective: the system learns from one semester of history plus faculty data, and it improves each time a schedule is accepted.

passages.section: Phase 5: Machine learning › Be honest about the data
passages.text:
One semester is a small dataset. The design starts with NLP and survey data, which need no history, then gives more weight to learned signals as evidence builds. Enrollment and section forecasting stay out of scope, as the quotation says.

The manuscript does not mention machine learning yet, so Q-17 is a follow-up for this phase. If faculty are preassigned before scheduling (Q-08), the fit model mainly checks assignments and suggests replacements. The module stays useful either way, because specialization is the interview's top-ranked challenge.

- [x] Build local embeddings for subject descriptions and faculty specialization or education (D-12)
- [x] Build features: text similarity, prior assignments, program match, qualification source
- [x] Train a regularized logistic regression, using historical assignments as positives and sampled pairs as negatives
- [x] Fall back to similarity ranking when there are too few examples
- [x] Store coefficients and metrics in `ModelVersion` (D-11)
- [x] Expose the ranking through `POST /v1/ml/recommend`

- [x] Build per-faculty day and time-band distributions from history, survey and Dean edits
- [x] Apply smoothing, so one observation cannot dominate, and decay older semesters
- [x] Keep declared preferences above inferred ones

Class scheduling in the College of Engineering at Manuel S. Enverga University Foundation involves coordinating faculty assignments, class times, rooms, laboratories, and section requirements. The existing spreadsheet-based process requires repeated checking and revisions. This study documented the current workflow and scheduling concerns and established requirements for ORDIQ, a proposed standalone, AI-based scheduling decision-support system. Using an applied, developmental research design, the study examined the department's scheduling process and gathered survey responses from 23 faculty members and 349 first- and second-year engineering students. The documented scheduling cycle lasted 47 days: 15 days for initial schedule preparation, 22 days for program-level rework combined with portal encoding, and 10 days for university-level review. Among faculty respondents, 22 of 23 (95.7%) perceived a need for significant improvement; classroom conflicts were the most frequently reported problem, selected 19 times. Among student respondents, 16.6% reported requesting a schedule adjustment during the current or most recently completed semester, most commonly to change a subject schedule. These survey findings are descriptive and should not be treated as representative of the entire college. The results informed a proposed system that validates scheduling data, checks mandatory time, faculty, room, and capacity constraints, and supports staff review of candidate schedules. Because system performance has not yet been established, this study does not claim reductions in scheduling time, rework, or student adjustment requests. The findings provide a local basis for developing and evaluating a constraint-based decision-support tool while retaining human review and institutional approval.
Keywords: academic timetabling, class scheduling, resource allocation, decision-support system, constraint-based scheduling, engineering education

Academic timetable preparation requires coordinated assignment of courses, sections, instructors, students, rooms, and time periods under institutional rules. At the College of Engineering, this work relies substantially on spreadsheet-based preparation and manual review before the schedule is encoded in the university portal. For the first semester for the academic year (A.Y.) 2026-2027, the college offers seven programs: Industrial, Civil, Electrical, Mechanical, Computer, Electronics, and Geodetic Engineering. Its 44 faculty members comprise 13 part-time, 18 full-time non-permanent, 12 full-time permanent, and one visiting lecturer. A feasible schedule must satisfy course duration, faculty specialization and availability, student numbers, room and laboratory capacity and type, and section needs. A conflict in time, room, or subject assignment can therefore trigger rework. Once completed, the schedule then proceeds to institutional verification and approval, which fall outside the scope of the proposed system.

A preliminary interview with the scheduling officer describes the current process as follows: The Dean prepares a raw first-semester schedule over 15 days, including weekends. Program coordinators then rework their respective program schedules, and all 44 faculty schedules were reportedly subject to rework for the first semester of academic year 2026 to 2027. This rework takes approximately one month of eight-hour weekdays. The reworked schedules are then encoded in the portal within a day every time a rework is finished. Student schedule changes add further workload: based on the scheduling officer's estimate, that about 70% of the 903 combined first- and second-year engineering students (632 students) request a change to their schedules.

A survey of 23 out of 44 faculty identified the main causes of rework. These fall into three groups: time-related causes (faculty availability and teaching load not properly considered, overlapping class schedules, and schedule hours that do not match required contact hours), room-related causes (double-booked rooms or laboratories, and room capacity or type that does not match the class), and subject-related causes (faculty specialization not matched to subjects, changes to assignments after the schedule is drafted, and outdated curriculum information). Most of these are incompatibilities that could, in principle, be detected before the schedule is encoded.

Therefore, the problem is not only constructing a timetable but repeatedly adjusting it. Searching manually for a compatible combination of instructor, room, and time slot is slow, and conflicts are found only after they have caused rework and results to unwanted situations including delays in schedule release, sudden changes in schedules for both faculty and students, and delay beginning of classes. The volume of student change requests suggests that released schedules often do not fit students' need due to multiple reasons including unwanted subject schedule or class time and found overlapping schedules or class conflicts.

Because rooms, laboratories, and faculty load are also assigned by hand, the resulting allocation may be feasible without being efficient in comparison to a release of a feasible schedule in less than a week with minor rework on the part of few program coordinators. Timetabling of this kind is a well-studied and computationally hard combinatorial problem [1], [2], and artificial intelligence (AI)-based techniques, such as genetic algorithms, tabu search, and constraint satisfaction have long been applied to it [3]. However, recent reviews observe that some methods are not fully utilized in real-world settings, possibly because of limited flexibility [2]. This suggests a need for systems configured to the rules and workflow of a specific institution.

This study addresses that need by developing an AI-based scheduling decision-support system for the College of Engineering. The system validates scheduling data, generates candidate schedules, and flags incompatible assignments before portal entry, while leaving exceptions and final approval to department staff. It also seeks to improve the allocation of rooms, laboratory spaces, and faculty load, and to respect scheduling preferences approved by the college. The study's contribution is a logically configured system, evaluated against a documented current-process baseline in terms of scheduling time, conflict count, rework effort, resource utilization, and the number of student schedule change request.

The main objective is to design, develop, and evaluate an AI-based automated scheduling system to support accurate and efficient class scheduling in the College of Engineering. Specifically, the study aims to:

1. To document the existing class-scheduling workflow, participants, inputs, constraints, correction types, and time requirements in the College of Engineering.

2. To analyze the causes of schedule rework, classified as time-, room-, and subject-related, to identify the constraints the system must detect and enforce.

3. To design and develop a standalone system that validates scheduling data, generates feasible candidate schedules, optimizes room utilization and faculty load distribution, prioritizes stakeholder-approved preferences, and flags conflicts for human review, and presents reports and a dashboard to support review and decision-making.

4. To evaluate the system in three stages:

4.1. Functional performance testing by the researchers;

4.2.Testing against the college's first-semester AY 2026-2027 scheduling data to assess schedule feasibility, resource utilization, and indicators of likely student change requests, and;

4.3. Pilot testing by the Dean to assess preparation effort, correction burden, and user experience, all against the prespecified criteria.

This study may benefit the following groups, subject to the conditions stated at the end of this section.

Dean and program coordinators. Automated generation and validation allow them to review candidate schedules and identify conflicts before schedules move to encoding. Rework currently takes half-a-month room, laboratory, subjects, time, and faculty scheduling plotting, combined with approximately one month of eight-hour weekdays, resulting to over 1.5-month scheduling process duration, so the study measure whether the system reduces this effort instead of assuming that it does.

Scheduling officer. May receive schedules that have undergone systematic pre-encoding checks for time, room, and subject conflicts. Portal entry and institutional approval remain outside the proposed system.

Faculty. Faculty may benefit if availability, teaching load, and subject specializations are presented accurately in the schedule, which addresses causes of rework identified in the survey.

Students. The study will also evaluate whether the system's schedules show fewer conflicts and unmet approved preferences, which may indicate a lower likelihood of student change requests.

The College of Engineering. The college may gain local evidence on the feasibility and operational value of a scheduling tool, including its effect on the use of rooms, laboratories, and faculty load and their specializations.

The University. The institution may adapt the proposed system once criteria and quality standards are met which can then be implemented on other college departments that may benefit the entire university in reducing scheduling efforts and minimizing conflicts in the overall process.

Future researchers and developers. The documented workflow, constraint classification, and evaluation criteria may serve as a reference for similar institution-specific scheduling systems.

These benefits depend on reliable input data, policy agreement, staff adoption, and satisfactory evaluation results. The study will also evaluate whether the system reduces the number of students who need to request schedule changes.

passages.section: 4. Introduction › 4.4 Scope and Limitations of the Study
passages.text: The scope of the study covers class scheduling for the seven programs of the College of Engineering (Civil, Computer, Electrical, Electronics, Geodetic, Industrial, and Mechanical Engineering) within the current College of Engineering building. The proposed AI-based scheduling decision-support system uses course and section records, room and laboratory characteristics (capacity and type), time periods, faculty assignments, specializations and availability, student or section requirements, and scheduling preferences approved by the department. Using these inputs, the system validates scheduling data, generates candidate schedules, and flags conflicts for human review. The system also provides reports and a dashboard summarizing conflicts, room and laboratory utilization, and faculty load to support review and decision-making. It does not process or accommodate individual student change requests. Instead, it aims to reduce their number by producing conflict-free schedules that reflect approved preferences. The system will be tested by the researchers, then with the college's first-semester A.Y. 2026-2027 scheduling data, and finally in a pilot test by the Dean to obtain experience-based feedback. The generated schedules are not released to the students and do not replace the college's official schedule. In addition, the application supports schedule preparation before submission to the university scheduling portal. It neither replaces nor directly integrates with that portal, and it does not automate the approval of the Registrar, the Audit Office, or the Vice President for Academic Affairs and Research.

passages.section: 4. Introduction › 4.4 Scope and Limitations of the Study
passages.text: System output is limited by the completeness and accuracy of local data and by the constraints encoded and approved by the department. Outdated curriculum information and changes to faculty, subject, section, or room assignments after a schedule is drafted can be handled only to the extent that the input data are updated, and the schedule is regenerated or adjusted. Conflicting requirements may require human decision, and the system cannot guarantee that every preference will be met. Additionally, some student changes requests arise from circumstances outside the schedule, such as individual situations, and cannot be addressed by the system. The department has no official record of the student schedule change requests, the baseline is the scheduling officer's estimate. Any comparison involving change requests is therefore indicative and not a statistically established reduction. Consequently, the gathering of data is also limited in terms of the constraints involving the faculty members' presence and amount of time to collect data during the time where they are outside the university attending important events. Likewise, the project does not include scheduling for other colleges or buildings nor other universities.

Fig. 1. Conceptual Framework of the AI-based scheduling decision-support system

The study uses an input–process–output (IPO) logic with a feedback loop. Inputs comprise validated course, section, and required contact-hour data; faculty specializations, availability, and teaching load; room and laboratory characteristics; available time periods; student and section data; and the college's scheduling rules and approved preferences. The process, carried out by the AI-based scheduling decision-support system, comprises data checking and validation; constraint encoding; candidate schedule generation and optimization; conflict detection and flagging; human review and revision; and feedback and iteration. The outputs are candidate class schedules, conflict and validation reports, a dashboard and reports that support review and decision-making, and documentation of assumptions, encoded rules, and validation records.

The system's provisional predictor is the availability of an automated, constraint-based scheduling capability. The provisional outcomes are: (a) process efficiency, measured through defined staff effort and elapsed preparation time, and (b) schedule quality, assessed through hard-constraint violations, correction counts, resource utilization, indicators of likely student change requests, and satisfaction of validated soft preferences. Mandatory rules must be met for a schedule to be feasible, while preferences can be prioritized only after college stakeholders agree on their weights. Human review supplies the feedback loop for correcting inputs, changing rules, or accepting documented exceptions. Portal encoding and final approval by the Registrar, the Audit Office, and the Vice President for Academic Affairs and Research remain outside the system. The system is evaluated against the documented current-process baseline in three stages: (1) researcher testing, (2) testing with the department's first-semester A.Y. 2026–2027 scheduling data, and (3) a pilot test by the Dean.

AI-based scheduling decision-support system. The proposed standalone application that validates scheduling inputs, generates candidate timetables, and identifies constraint conflicts for authorized review. It supports, and does not replace, human decisions and institutional approval.

Candidate schedule. A timetable produced by the system for review by the Dean and program coordinators. It is not an approved schedule until accepted through the college's and the university's own procedures.

Correction burden. The amount of rework needed after a schedule is drafted, measured by the number of conflicts or corrections, the staff time spent on them, and indicators of likely students change requests.

Dashboard. A visual summary within the system conflicts, room and laboratory utilization, faculty load, and validation status, intended to help authorized users review candidate schedules and make decisions.

Faculty load distribution. The spread of teaching assignments across faculty members, assessed using measures finalized during requirements analysis.

Hard constraint. A mandatory scheduling rule that a feasible timetable must satisfy, such as preventing a room or faculty member from being assigned to overlapping classes.

Optimization. In this study, the improvement of schedule quality and resource utilization relative to the documented current-process baseline. It does not imply a mathematically global optimum.

Pilot testing. A trial in which the Dean uses the system with the college's first-semester AY 2026-2027 scheduling data, without releasing the generated schedules for official use, to assess the system's usability and to obtain feedback.

Resource utilization. The extent to which rooms, laboratories, and faculty time are used within available capacity, assessed using measures finalized during requirements analysis.

Schedule feasibility. The state in which all encoded hard constraints are satisfied. It does not by itself establish that preferences or schedule quality are optimal.

Schedule quality. The degree to which a feasible schedule meets approved soft preferences and planning objectives, assessed using measures finalized during requirements analysis.

Scheduling-process effort. Staff time attributable to schedule preparation and correction, recorded using a defined start and end rule and expressed in person-hours.

Soft constraint. A desirable but nonmandatory preference, such as avoiding a less-preferred time, whose priority must be set by the department.

passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies
passages.text: This section reviews the theories, research, patents, standards, and existing systems relevant to an AI-based scheduling decision-support system for the College of Engineering. It establishes the technical foundation for a constraint-based, feasibility-first design, examines how published studies and available technologies treat scheduling constraints, workload, and schedule quality, and identifies the local gap that the project intends to address.

passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies › 5.1 Theoretical and Technical Foundations
passages.text:
University course timetabling is a constrained allocation problem: teaching events must be assigned to periods and rooms while respecting faculty specializations and availability, section requirements, and institutional rules. These decisions are interdependent, so a locally acceptable assignment can make another event infeasible. Timetabling surveys describe the complexity of hard and soft constraints and review exact, metaheuristic, and hybrid approaches [2], [3]. For this proposal, "AI-based" refers to constraint-based search and optimization; it does not imply machine learning.

Each required class event is assigned a time period, a room, and a qualified instructor. Hard constraints encode mandatory requirements:

- A room cannot host simultaneous classes.
- A faculty member or section cannot be assigned to overlapping events.
- Each event must receive its required duration and meeting pattern.
- A laboratory course must use a suitable laboratory room.
- Class size cannot exceed room capacity.

The college must confirm additional rules, including teaching periods, faculty-subject specializations, and weekly meeting patterns, before they are encoded. Missing or outdated rules can produce a technically feasible but unacceptable candidate. If the input constraints are infeasible, the system should report the cause rather than silently relax a mandatory rule.

passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies › 5.1 Theoretical and Technical Foundations
passages.text:
Soft constraints represent preferences that may be traded off only after stakeholder approval. Candidate examples in this proposal include preferred faculty periods, avoiding evening classes for lower-year sections where feasible, minimizing excessive gaps, balancing room use, and distributing faculty load. Constraint-handling approaches distinguish mandatory rules from preferences [4]. The final set and priority of soft constraints remain subject to requirements analysis; no preference should override a hard constraint without an authorized, documented exception.

Mixed-integer programming can represent assignment and resource constraints explicitly. Rappos et al. used a feasible-solution stage followed by local improvement in a competition problem that also included student-to-class allocation [5]. That benchmark design is informative about staged optimization, but individual student allocation is outside this proposal's scope. A suitable design sequence is to seek hard-constraint feasibility first, then improve candidates against stakeholder-approved preferences.

passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies › 5.1 Theoretical and Technical Foundations
passages.text: The system should make candidate assignments, detected conflicts, unmet preferences, and the reasons for each warning reviewable. Multi-criteria timetabling research illustrates that criteria and decision levels can differ; some models also include individual student assignments, which this project excludes [6]. Whether the prototype uses a lexicographic hierarchy or agreed weights must be decided during requirements analysis and documented for staff review. The technical foundation is therefore a transparent constraint model, feasibility checks, preference-based improvement after stakeholder approval, and human review.

passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies › 5.2 Review of Related Literature
passages.text:
Automated scheduling. Automated timetabling research includes exact models, constraint-based methods, metaheuristics, and hybrids. The university course-timetabling survey by Chen et al. describes the prevalence of metaheuristic and hybrid approaches and notes that limited flexibility may constrain uptake in real-world settings [2], [3]. This literature supports explicit local rule encoding and testing; it does not establish which solver will fit this college or prove that automation alone improves schedule quality.

Constraint-handling. Constraint-handling rules provide one way to represent mandatory conditions and preferences within a scheduling approach [4]. Mixed-integer programming provides another explicit formulation: Rappos et al. report a feasible-first method followed by local improvement and benchmark performance in the International Timetabling Competition 2019 [5]. The competition result is computational evidence for those instances, not evidence of local usability, staff-time savings, or fit with the department's rules.

passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies › 5.2 Review of Related Literature
passages.text:
Customization. Customization matters because institutions differ in their constraints and workflows. Algethami and Laesanklang model faculty-course assignments, specializations, preferences, and workload in a pre-registration setting [7]. Dunke and Nickel examine customized multi-level, multi-criteria planning, including individual assignments [6]. These studies help identify possible dimensions for requirements analysis, but the proposed prototype remains at the section, faculty, and room level and does not allocate individual students.

Algorithm performance. Algorithm studies report results on defined instances rather than end-to-end administrative outcomes. Song et al. found feasible solutions for 58 of 60 benchmark instances with an iterated local-search method [8]; Thepphakorn and Pongcharoen compared Cuckoo Search strategies on 11 engineering-faculty instances [9]. Such results demonstrate computational approaches in their tested settings only. They do not establish that either method is suitable for the department's data or that a particular runtime translates into reduced coordinator effort.

passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies › 5.2 Review of Related Literature
passages.text:
Operational efficiency. Evidence about operational efficiency should be separated from solver performance. Abdennadher and Marte describe a Munich prototype and report minutes of processing compared with manual days in that setting [4]. Stallaert reports an operational university case in which administrators used automated scheduling for three years and described comparable schedules as being prepared faster than manually [10]. Both are context-specific reports; neither provides a local estimate for this department. The present evaluation should therefore record elapsed time and person-hours by process stage, alongside solver runtime and correction effort.

Real-world scheduling cases. Real-world problem descriptions also differ in their decision scope and data. Rudová, Müller, and Müllerová analyze 30 competition cases combining student sectioning with time and room assignment [11]. Their work illustrates variation across institutions, but those benchmark cases are not a direct comparator for a single college's pre-portal workflow. The proposed evaluation should use locally verified rules and a documented current-process baseline.

passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies › 5.2 Review of Related Literature
passages.text:
Schedule-quality measures. Studies of schedule quality provide candidate measures rather than a ready-made local objective. Tavakoli et al. report a course-timetabling case study using lecturer and course-related measures [12]. Palma and Bornhardt consider section balance and schedule flexibility in a curriculum-based model, including a real-case comparison with a manual schedule [13]. These examples make section balance and preference satisfaction reasonable topics for stakeholder review, but their case-specific results should not be generalized to this project.

Faculty and room constraints. Faculty assignments, room suitability, capacity, and time conflicts are directly relevant to the department's stated scheduling problem. Research on faculty-course assignment constraints supports representing specializations, availability, and load explicitly [7]. The literature does not determine the college's preferred load distribution or establish that any one measure should dominate. The system should report feasibility separately from preference satisfaction, and staff should review any trade-offs.

passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies › 5.2 Review of Related Literature
passages.text:
Schedule-quality criteria. Schedule quality is multidimensional. A candidate must first satisfy approved hard constraints; among feasible candidates, stakeholders may consider room and laboratory suitability, faculty availability and workload, section conflicts, and approved preferences. The preliminary faculty survey and scheduling-officer interview identify local issues for investigation, but neither establishes population-level priorities or a validated weighting scheme.

Fairness. Fairness may also matter if the department identifies a defensible objective, such as the distribution of undesirable time periods. Mühlenthaler and Wanka study the distribution of undesirable soft-constraint violations in academic timetabling [14]. Their work motivates asking stakeholders whether such a criterion is relevant; it does not mean that this proposal has selected a fairness measure or defined the groups to compare.

passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies › 5.2 Review of Related Literature
passages.text:
Student-level allocation. This study does not optimize individual student schedules. Research that combines student sectioning with room and time assignment [11] or considers individual courses of study [6] addresses a broader or later allocation stage. Here, section-level enrollment and year information may inform candidate schedules, but the prototype will not assign named or individual students to sections. Any future expansion would require separate requirements, data, privacy review, and evaluation.

Evaluation measures. Accordingly, evaluation should distinguish hard-constraint violations from unmet soft preferences, documented exceptions, resource-use measures, and staff correction effort. Benchmark feasibility, solver speed, or an aggregate score alone would not establish operational benefit. The definitions of errors, approved preferences, and any group-level comparisons must be settled with college stakeholders before testing.

Local validation. The literature provides design options and candidate evaluation dimensions, not a predetermined solver, objective weight, or expected benefit. The local study must verify its input data, confirm the department's rules, document the current workflow, and test whether staff can interpret and use the generated reports. No reduction in preparation time, rework, or student change requests is claimed before evaluation.

passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies › 5.4 Applicable Engineering Standards and Regulations
passages.text:
ISO/IEC 25010:2023 and ISO/IEC 25012:2008 may guide the selection of software- and data-quality criteria relevant to the proposed scheduling decision-support system [17], [18]. The evaluation will use criteria that are relevant to the prototype and defined as observable measures in the methods section—for example, correct handling of approved scheduling constraints, validation of input data, and system response time.

ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 may guide how stakeholder needs and system requirements are elicited, documented, and checked for consistency [19]. The research team will tailor this guidance to the project's scope, including the college's approved scheduling rules and reporting needs.

The project will consider applicable university quality procedures under the university's ISO 9001-based quality-management system [20]. This may include documenting approved requirements and scheduling rules, recording validation and test results, and tracking revisions, exceptions, and corrective actions. passages.section: 5. Review of Literature and Related Studies › 5.6 Synthesis of the Review
passages.text: The reviewed literature supports investigating a transparent, feasibility-first scheduling process that separates mandatory constraints from stakeholder-approved preferences and leaves final review to college staff. Published algorithm results concern their tested instances; operational reports are limited to the institutions studied [4], [8]–[10]. Other work helps identify faculty-assignment, section-balance, and possible fairness dimensions [7], [13], [14], while competition cases show that timetabling problems vary across institutions [11]. Preliminary patent records are examples only [15], [16]. The proposal's listed standards require edition and applicability checks before detailed use [17]–[20], and data handling requires institutional review under applicable law [21]. The local gap is to translate verified college rules into a standalone pre-portal decision-support prototype and evaluate feasibility, preference satisfaction, resource use, preparation effort, corrections, and user experience against a documented baseline.

The study is applied research because it responds to a documented local scheduling problem, and developmental research because it will design, build, and evaluate a software system. The work will proceed from descriptive process analysis to requirements specification, iterative prototype development, and system evaluation. At proposal stage, only the scheduling-officer interview figures have been supplied; faculty and student baseline data and the proposed system's performance results are not yet available.

Evaluation should compare the current process with system-assisted scheduling on the same or closely matched schedule inputs where feasible. If a single semester's data and schedule cycle are available, use paired comparisons at the schedule or program level; otherwise report descriptive prototype tests and usability findings without implying a causal effect.

The study is situated in the College of Engineering at Manuel S. Enverga University Foundation (MSEUF), Lucena City. The system scope is the seven programs and the current College of Engineering building. Department personnel prepare schedules through the existing spreadsheet-based workflow and submit schedules to the university's official portal for encoding and subsequent institutional review. Program coordinators, the Dean, scheduling personnel, faculty, and students are relevant stakeholders. The application is planned as a standalone tool used before portal encoding.

The procedure for this study followed a systematic, step-by-step process, beginning with the collection of relevant information and the identification and analysis of existing class scheduling problems. Based on the findings, appropriate solutions were formulated, and a development plan for the decision-support system was established. The process then proceeded to the system's design and development, followed by implementation and validation to assess its functionality and effectiveness in addressing the identified scheduling problems.
