The proposed design is an AI-assisted, spreadsheet-based class scheduling decision-support system for the College of Engineering, named ORDIQ, with the tagline "Order Meets Intelligence." The system is designed to support the preparation, checking, generation, and review of class schedules while retaining authorized personnel's responsibility for reviewing and approving the final timetable.

Fig. 3. ORDIQ Application Logo

Figure 3 illustrates the ORDIQ logo combines a calendar and a stylized artificial intelligence brain to represent the integration of class scheduling and intelligent decision support. The maroon and orange color scheme establishes the application's visual identity, while the calendar symbolizes timetable organization, and the brain represents AI-assisted analysis and decision-making. These elements reflect the system's tagline, "Order Meets Intelligence."

1. Overview of the Proposed System

The proposed system will be developed as a standalone scheduling application featuring a spreadsheet-based workspace, an integrated AI Assistant, a dashboard, and reporting functions. Its interface will provide centralized access to academic data and scheduling tools, allowing authorized users to manage scheduling information, identify conflicts, generate candidate timetables, and review resource allocation. The application will support both the validation of existing schedules and the generation of alternative schedules based on approved constraints. Final approval and encoding into the existing academic portal will remain outside the system's direct scope.

2. Spreadsheet-Based Workspace

The main workspace will organize faculty, courses and sections, rooms and laboratories, time periods, and schedules into editable tables. The faculty data view will include information such as faculty identification, specialization, teaching load, availability, preferences, and status. Data-entry controls, search, filtering, and import and export options will support the management and review of scheduling records. Validation rules will identify missing, invalid, or inconsistent information before schedule generation.

Fig. 4. Proposed ORDIQ Application Interface

Figure 4 shows the proposed interface presents the system's main dashboard, spreadsheet-based data workspace, weekly schedule preview, system analytics, and integrated AI Assistant. The navigation sidebar provides access to faculty, courses and sections, rooms and laboratories, schedules, rules and preferences, and reports. Dashboard indicators summarize scheduling information, while the AI Assistant supports users in identifying conflicts and requesting schedule improvements.

The interface is designed to consolidate scheduling activities within a single workspace. The spreadsheet-based layout supports the management and review of academic data, while the dashboard and analytics provide an overview of scheduling conditions. The AI Assistant complements these functions by helping users interpret issues and access scheduling operations. Together, these components are intended to support a more organized scheduling process while retaining human review and approval of final schedules.

3. Integrated AI Assistant

A persistent AI Assistant panel will be positioned beside the main workspace, allowing users to issue supported natural-language commands without leaving the current view. Users may request conflict checks, workload summaries, explanations of scheduling issues, room-utilization reviews, and candidate schedule generation. The AI Assistant will interpret requests and explain results, while the constraint-based scheduling engine will perform the actual validation and timetable-generation operations. Changes to important records and schedules will require user review and confirmation.

4. Dashboard and Reporting Functions

The dashboard will provide an overview of scheduling status through indicators such as the number of classes scheduled, detected conflicts, faculty workload balance, and room utilization. The finalized interface will also include a weekly timetable preview, system analytics, and a summary of conflicts requiring attention. Reporting functions will present validation findings, candidate schedules, unresolved constraints, and scheduling summaries. Displayed indicators will be based on available data and defined calculation methods; illustrative values in the design mockup will not be treated as verified results.

5. Proposed System Architecture

The system will consist of connected components for data management, validation, scheduling, user interaction, reporting, and export. The spreadsheet workspace will manage academic records, the validation module will check data quality, and the constraint-based scheduling engine will evaluate existing schedules and generate candidate timetables. The AI Assistant will interpret user requests and explain results, while the dashboard and reporting module will present relevant indicators and findings. An export module will prepare reviewed schedules for encoding into the existing academic portal. The application will operate independently without assuming direct portal integration.

6. Scheduling Constraints and Priorities

The scheduling engine will distinguish between hard constraints and soft preferences. Hard constraints, such as faculty availability, faculty and room conflicts, room capacity and suitability, required course contact hours, and approved calendar restrictions, must be satisfied for a schedule to be considered feasible. Soft preferences, such as preferred teaching periods and workload distribution, may be used to compare feasible alternatives based on priorities approved by the department. If no feasible schedule can be generated, the system will report the limitation rather than silently relax mandatory requirements.

7. Proposed User Workflow

The proposed workflow will begin with entering or importing academic data, followed by data validation and the checking of existing schedules or generation of candidate timetables. The system will display conflicts, unmet preferences, and other relevant findings through the spreadsheet workspace, dashboard, AI Assistant, and reports. Authorized users may correct data, revise scheduling criteria, and compare alternatives before reviewing and approving a selected schedule. The approved timetable may then be exported for encoding into the existing portal.

8. Data Management, Export, and User Control

The system will use structured records to support consistent validation of faculty, courses, sections, rooms, and schedules. Import and export functions will be designed according to the data formats required by the department. Access to scheduling information will be limited to authorized users, and the application will distinguish original records from proposed changes and generated schedules. Important changes will require confirmation to support data integrity and human oversight.

9. System Evaluation and Validation

The proposed system will be evaluated through functional testing, testing using available first-semester Academic Year 2026–2027 scheduling data, and pilot testing with the Dean or other authorized personnel. Evaluation may consider schedule feasibility, conflict detection, faculty workload compliance, room utilization, schedule preparation and revision effort, and user-perceived usability. Performance claims will be based on defined evaluation criteria and actual test results rather than the visual interface alone.

10. Design Decisions Requiring Confirmation

The final implementation will require confirmation of the department's mandatory scheduling constraints, preference priorities, spreadsheet fields, AI Assistant permissions, import and export formats, user access requirements, and evaluation criteria. These details will be established with the appropriate department personnel and project supervisor before implementation.

This section presents and discusses the findings from the interviews, documented scheduling workflow, time-study records, and surveys administered to faculty members and first- and second-year engineering students. The results are examined in relation to the study objectives of documenting the existing scheduling process, identifying recurring scheduling problems and their potential causes, and deriving requirements for an AI-based scheduling decision-support system. The findings describe the current process and provide a basis for system design and subsequent evaluation; they do not establish that the proposed system has already improved scheduling performance.

1. Existing Process and Challenges of Department Scheduling

The existing scheduling process was examined through interviews with the Dean and scheduling officer and review of the recorded workflow. The analysis focused on the sequence of schedule preparation, portal encoding, conflict checking, program-level revisions, and university-level review. These findings were used to identify the operational constraints that should be addressed by the proposed decision-support system.

Fig. 5. Current Scheduling Process of the Department

Figure 5 illustrates the existing scheduling process of the College of Engineering, as documented through interviews with the department dean and scheduling officer. The process begins with the dean manually preparing the department schedule using Microsoft Excel, considering faculty specialization and availability, course subjects, time blocks, classrooms, and laboratories. The schedule is then forwarded to the scheduling officer, who encodes the information into the university portal and manually checks for scheduling conflicts. When conflicts are detected, the scheduling officer notifies the concerned program coordinators, who manually revise their respective program schedules. The revised information is then returned for further processing and checking. Once no conflicts are detected, the schedule report is submitted through the portal for review by the Registrar, followed by endorsement to the Audit Department and the Office of the Vice President for Academic and Research Affairs (OVPAR). The university processors then verify the submitted schedule and determine whether it is accepted. If the schedule is rejected, the department must make the necessary revisions and resubmit the report, potentially extending the overall processing time. These review and verification stages follow established procedures and processing periods that are beyond the department's direct control.

The interviews further revealed three major challenges that contribute to the complexity and delays of the existing scheduling process, ranked by the department dean and scheduling officer as follows: (1) faculty specialization, (2) time gaps between subjects, and (3) classroom and laboratory utilization based on capacity.

Faculty specialization. Faculty specialization was identified as the most challenging scheduling consideration because each faculty member must be assigned subjects aligned with their qualifications and area of specialization. Differences in faculty teaching loads, specializations, and assigned subject types further complicate the allocation process, requiring considerable effort to develop a feasible schedule.

Time gaps between subjects. Unexpected gaps between subjects may become apparent after schedules have been prepared or published, requiring further adjustments. The scheduling officer also reported that students may begin enrolling while the schedules are still being encoded into the academic portal. This situation creates additional constraints because enrollment may begin before the schedules have been finalized, potentially complicating subsequent revisions.

Classroom and laboratory utilization based on capacity. Another challenge involves assigning student sections to appropriate classrooms and laboratories according to enrollment and room capacity. Based on the information gathered, lecture rooms accommodate at least 40 students, while laboratory rooms accommodate at least 30 students. Although the department considers its available facilities sufficient, the limited number of rooms requires careful coordination of room assignments, student sections, and time slots to avoid conflicts and capacity-related issues.

Taken together, these findings suggest that the primary improvement opportunity lies in optimizing the scheduling and allocation of existing academic resources rather than simply increasing the number of available rooms. Improving the coordination of faculty assignments, subject time slots, student sections, and room utilization may reduce scheduling conflicts and unnecessary revisions. A decision-support system that identifies potential conflicts before submission could help the department prepare more accurate schedules and minimize avoidable rework. However, the university's required review and verification stages would remain necessary, and their established processing periods would still need to be considered in the overall scheduling timeline.

Research on university course timetabling describes scheduling as a constrained allocation problem in which multiple requirements must be considered together [22]. In the College of Engineering, these requirements include faculty specialization and availability, teaching assignments, room and laboratory capacity, section schedules, and required contact hours. A decision-support system could help staff identify conflicts before portal submission. However, the extent to which it reduces preparation time or revisions must be established through testing against the documented manual baseline. The reported causes span time, room, and subject-related constraints. Time-related selections included overlapping schedules involving faculty, year levels, or sections (15), faculty availability or teaching load not being properly considered (12), and schedule hours not matching required contact hours (six). Room-related selections included room or laboratory availability and double-booking (14), and a mismatch between room capacity or type and the class or subject (12). Subject-related selections included changes in faculty, subject, section, or room after the draft schedule was prepared (15), outdated or incorrect subject information (seven), and faculty-specialization mismatch (six). Since these were multiple-response items, the counts are not mutually exclusive. Collectively, they support the need for reliable input data, early conflict checking, and revalidation whenever an affected assignment changes.

Synthesis and implications for system requirements

The results identify recurring problems involving room conflicts, schedule errors, time lapses, workload and availability, required contact hours, and changes to scheduling information after the initial draft. The interviews emphasize faculty specialization as a difficult planning constraint, while faculty respondents most frequently reported classroom conflicts. These findings are not necessarily contradictory: the interviews describe perceived difficulty in constructing the overall timetable, whereas the survey records problems experienced by individual faculty members. The system should prioritize mandatory constraint checking, data validation, and revalidation after changes. The study should evaluate the prototype using documented criteria such as the number of detected conflicts, the number of unresolved hard-constraint violations, the number of revisions required, preparation and review time, and user feedback. No performance improvement should be claimed until these measures have been tested against the existing process.

In summary, the findings have several limitations. The faculty survey included 23 of 44 faculty members, and the student survey covered first- and second-year students only. The reported 16.6% student schedule-change result differs from the scheduling officer's approximate 70% estimate, and the available information does not establish that the figures use the same definition, population, or reporting period. The time-study record also combines schedule rework and portal encoding into a single 22-day entry, preventing the duration of each activity from being separated. These limitations should be considered when interpreting the results and when designing the subsequent system evaluation.

Further, the results describe a manual, multi-stage scheduling process with a recorded duration of 47 days and recurring problems associated with time, room, and subject constraints. The findings support developing a decision-support system that assists authorized personnel in validating scheduling data and identifying conflicts before submission. The system's actual effect on preparation time, rework, and schedule quality must be determined through functional testing and comparison with the documented manual baseline.
